runs.goal_hypothesis: Establish a 15.36M-step 0.25 block-reward control for shaping and defensive-opening refinements.

results_insights.insight: The long 0.25 control reached 24.17% average win rate.

reasoning: Longer 0.25 block-reward training yielded moderate average and a nonzero robustness floor.
The strongest evidence was defensive-side competence rather than uniformly high policy performance.
This baseline changes horizon and learning-rate schedule versus earlier sweeps, so cross-group causal comparisons are confounded.

runs.goal_hypothesis: Test whether slight potential shaping improves long 0.25 block-reward training.

results_insights.insight: Shaping reduced average win rate by 7.83 percentage points versus control.
Defensive-X halved from 46% to 23%, with 32.63-move games.
Longer defensive games did not translate into more wins.

reasoning: Slight shaping was harmful under the long 0.25 block-reward regimen.
The one-knob comparison and consistent average/floor declines make shaping the leading explanation.
Single-seed variance remains, and training diagnostics show a slightly different realized mean block reward.

runs.goal_hypothesis: Test whether raising defensive-opening probability from 0.3 to 0.4 improves long 0.25 block-reward training.

results_insights.insight: More openings improved average win rate by 4.5 percentage points.
The floor was 6%, essentially preserving the control's 7%.
Offensive-X improved from 29% to 45%, over 10.56-move games.
The offensive-X gain came with slightly shorter games.

reasoning: Increasing defensive openings modestly improved aggregate performance without sacrificing the floor materially.
The gain unexpectedly included offensive-X competence, suggesting broader curriculum benefit.
The one-knob comparison is strong evidence, but 100-game evaluation and single seeds leave sampling uncertainty.
